newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt markets end weaker on political jitters.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt markets end weaker on political jitters.

* Looming election undermines NZ debt markets at close
* Sentiment increasingly bearish ahead of Saturday's vote
* Market seen drifting in week ahead
Bearish sentiment undermined the performance of New Zealand debt markets at Tuesday's close as a nervous market contemplated the possibility of a left-wing coalition in government.
The afternoon saw trade quieten down after a morning of moderate selling, with a few bonds coming back in from offshore.
Dealers put the morning's weakness down largely to a televised political leaders' debate on Monday night, the last before a general election on Saturday.

The reactions to the leaders of a group of 120 undecided voters were monitored in a wiggly line graph dubbed "the worm", which judged opposition Labour party leader Helen Clark to be the debate's winner.
Conservative National party leader and Prime Minister Jim Bolger did not score well.

"He's been doing disastrously in the polls...He didn't even need to talk and the worm took a dive, so you could call that good news for Clark. There is just a generally bearish view of Helen Clark's worm," one dealer said.
Recent political polls have shown Labour and its potential left-wing coalition partners dramatically closing the gap on the ruling conservative National Party.
Dealers said poor sentiment was compounded by weakness in the currency, and 90-day bank bills had traded to a high of 10.02 percent before closing around 9.99 percent.

December futures contracts were given in the morning but came back better bid in the afternoon, to finish off 19 points at 90.46. Overnight cash was up at 10.05 percent from its 9.95 percent close on Monday.
Bond yields finished higher across the curve, with the shorter maturities off around five or six basis points and longer bonds off around 12.
Dealers expect the market to drift around current levels for the rest of the week, following currency movements and further developments in the political arena.
One dealer said the market was pricing in uncertainty continuing for at least a couple of months.

"On Monday if Clark does win a majority of the seats but not a total majority, nobody's really going to know what will happen, who she's in a coalition with, whether they've had discussions on Sunday, whether anything's cemented, and how much clout the (left-wing) Alliance has got.

"You're obviously going to see a little bit of strength if National gets in just because of the turn in sentiment, but I can't see it going far if Labour gets in either because people have to know what's going to happen first," he said.
